To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the preference of children for one dimension of a compound stimulus was controlled by the pairing of the stimulus with a conditioned positive reinforcer.

(a) the preference of children for the dimension of a sample stimulus that was paired with reinforcement was greater than the preference for the nonpaired dimension, and (b) this effect was obtained for both the color and form dimensions, but was not obtained for the two other stimuli.
(1) a stimulus that precedes reinforcement can be a conditioned positive reinforcer for children, and (2) this effect can be demonstrated in a preference measure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the conditioned reinforcing function of a paired stimulus upon the preference for one of two stimuli.
the effects of conditioned positive reinforcement on the preference of children for a stimulus.
preference in children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the preference measure employed in this study was sensitive to conditioned positive reinforcement, but that the magnitude of this effect was variable among subjects.
the results of the present experiment are consistent with the hypothesis that a stimulus that precedes a reinforcer will become a conditioned positive reinforcer.
the paired stimulus controlled preference, but only for some children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the conditioned positive reinforcing effect of a stimulus can be demonstrated with children in a preference measure.

a stimulus preceding reinforcement can acquire conditioned positive reinforcing function, but the magnitude and generality of this function is dependent upon the individual subject and the specific stimulus-reinforcement contingencies.
the paired stimulus was effective in producing a preference, regardless of the match dimension on which it was dependent or the identity of the paired stimulus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
preference can be conditioned and controlled by positive reinforcement.
children's preference for a stimulus can be controlled by the conditioned reinforcing effect of that stimulus.
the use of a preference measure is an efficient method for assessing the reinforcing function of stimuli.
